what: Michael D. Kelly's Stanford AI Project thesis (AIM-130) described a program that picked out, from TV-camera pictures of people, those showing the same person, using automatically extracted head outlines and body/face measurements.
fit: A computer, working from TV-camera images with no human marking of features, matched people's pictures against a collection of stored pictures to decide which depicted the same person.

sources.title: Project Technical Report (A.I. Memo abstracts, incl. AIM-130 Visual Identification of People by Computer)
sources.quote: pictures of people taken by a TV camera, those pictures that depict the same person

sources.title: Facial recognition system
sources.quote: In 1970, Takeo Kanade publicly demonstrated a face-matching system that located anatomical features

note: Second pass chose Kanade 1970 (Wikipedia). Kelly's July 1970 Stanford thesis is a contemporary, fully computer-based face-matching system of the same year, so the year is unchanged but the source is now contemporary. Earlier candidate: Bledsoe, Chan and Bisson / Panoramic Research 'man-machine' face recognition (proposal Jan 1963, work 1964-66): the computer matched stored feature distances, but a human had to locate features on photographs by tablet, no camera, so rejected as not automated. Kanade's own thesis is 1973, later. Month is the thesis month; the Jan 1970 AIM-108 head-outline paper is its precursor.
searched: archive.org full-text (ia_search3) for 'face recognition' 1960-75, 'Bledsoe facial recognition' 1960-75, 'Visual identification of people by computer' 1969-73; page_text3 on DTIC AD0724867 and AD0776233; Wikipedia Facial recognition system. DTIC AD0713252 (the thesis itself) has no OCR text; Google Books unavailable.

what: By 1994 facial-recognition biometric products had reached the marketplace (access control); the DMV offices of West Virginia and New Mexico followed, using automated face recognition against duplicate licences after the 1993 FERET test.
fit: Commercial systems used cameras and computers to match a person's face against an enrolled stored image for entry control and identity checks.

sources.title: Biometric Identification Verification Technology Status and Feasibility Study
sources.quote: Systems which have reached the marketplace include fingerprint, thumbprint, hand geometry, keystroke dynamics, signature dynamics, voice patterns, retina patterns, and facial recognition.

sources.title: Facial recognition system
sources.quote: became the first DMV offices to use automated facial recognition systems to prevent people from obtaining multiple driving licenses

note: Replaces second pass 1997 (ZN-Face sale). The 1994 DTIC study says facial recognition products were already on the market but names no deployment and calls them unreliable (it judged them unable to meet DoD needs), so the date is the earliest documented market presence, not a documented first user. The DMV use (West Virginia, New Mexico) is after 1993 but I found no dated source. Mexico 2000 and Super Bowl 2001 are later.
searched: ia_search3 'face recognition' driver license 1993-99, Viisage / Visionics / Miros 1994-99, 'facial recognition' police/casino 1990-96; Wikipedia Facial recognition system; websearch for first DMV use (no dated source). SPIE 1996 law-enforcement proceedings and Encyclopedia of Emerging Industries not readable (lending, 401).

what: Apple announced Face ID on the iPhone X (September 2017), putting face recognition unlock on a mass-market phone.
fit: A camera and processor match the user's face against a stored face model to unlock the phone and authorise purchases.

sources.title: Face ID
sources.quote: Apple announced Face ID alongside the iPhone X on September 12, 2017

note: Kept from second pass. Earlier consumer face matching existed: Android 4.0 Face Unlock (2011), photo-tagging suggestions in consumer photo software and social networks (c.2009-2010), but I could not fetch dated sources for them; Face ID is the date of introduction, not a measured adoption figure.
searched: Wikipedia Face ID; Apple newsroom page timed out; no usage-share source found.

concept_note: First demonstration kept at 1970 but re-sourced to Kelly's contemporary Stanford thesis (Kanade's system is a Wikipedia claim); first practical use moved earlier from 1997 to 1994 on a contemporary DTIC study (low confidence); mass adoption unchanged (2017).

what: Wolfgang von Kempelen of Vienna published Le mécanisme de la parole with a description of his bellows-driven speaking machine, which he said pronounced several hundred Latin, French and Italian words.
fit: A machine (bellows, reed and shaped resonator worked by an operator's hands) generated whole spoken words with an artificial voice, not just isolated vowels.

sources.publisher: B. Bauer, Vienna (digitised by Wellcome Library)
sources.title: Le mécanisme de la parole, suivi de la description d'une machine parlante
sources.quote: Enfin je l'ai portée au point y que je lui fais prononcer dâbordy & fans excep- tioUy tous les mots latins

sources.title: Speech synthesis
sources.quote: There followed the bellows-operated "acoustic-mechanical speech machine" of Wolfgang von Kempelen of Pressburg, Hungary, described in a 1791 paper.

note: Same date as the second pass, now with the contemporary book itself (Kempelen's preface says he had worked on it for many years, so a working machine existed before 1791, but no dated earlier demonstration was found; Wikipedia's Kempelen page says 1789 for the book, the printed title page says 1791). Earlier candidates: Kratzenstein 1779-80 resonators making five vowels only (rejected, not speech); Abbe Mical's 'talking heads' of c.1778-83 (no fetchable source). Later: Voder 1939, Kelly-Gerstman IBM 7090 1961, Umeda 1968 text-to-speech. A hand-operated machine counts as the artificial voice; the definition does not require a computer.
searched: archive.org full text 'Kempelen machine parlante / sprechende Maschine' 1778-1800; Mical talking heads 1778-1800 (0 hits); page_text3 on the 1791 French edition, the 1783 Lettres sur le joueur d'echecs (no mention) and Wikipedia Kempelen and Speech synthesis.

what: The Kurzweil Reading Machine (scanner plus Votrax synthesizer reading printed pages aloud to blind people) was introduced in early 1976, the same year as Telesensory Systems' Speech+ talking calculator for the blind.
fit: A computer converted text into phonetic commands for an electronic voice synthesizer that spoke the text aloud, for blind users' real reading needs.

sources.title: Kurzweil Reading Machine article (Cambridge, Mass.)
sources.quote: A computerized desktop machine that “reads” printed pages to blind people has been introduced by a small research firm here.

sources.title: Speech synthesis
sources.quote: One of the first was the Telesensory Systems Inc. (TSI) Speech+ portable calculator for the blind in 1976.

note: Date unchanged. Considered earlier: Votrax voice synthesizer sold from 1972 (Computerworld 1972-11-29 'Votrax synthesizer set for speaking debut', for telephone inquiry-voice response, and a Votrax User's Group of 26 owners by Oct 1974), but the owners' newsletter shows mostly research and hobby use and I found no documented end-user service before 1976; Umeda 1968 and MUSA 1975 were lab systems. Because Votrax units were being bought and used from 1972-74, a practical use before 1976 is possible but not documented.
searched: ia_search3 'Votrax speech/voice synthesizer' 1970-76 (computerworld) and 'Votrax installed/using/users' 1972-75; bitsavers Federal Screw Works Votrax manual (1973) and VUG Newsletter 1 (1974-10); Kurzweil reading machine 1973-77.

what: Texas Instruments' Speak & Spell (introduced June 1978) put a speech-synthesiser chip in a child's hand-held toy; by 1980-81 it was an ordinary household device.
fit: An electronic device generated spoken words with an artificial voice (TMC0280 linear-predictive speech synthesizer) to talk to ordinary users, though only from stored words, not arbitrary text.

sources.title: Implications of Hand Held Electronic Games and Microcomputers for Informal Learning
sources.quote: the gane presents questions and provides feedback with a synthesized voice, a unique application of mi- croelectronic technology in hand held games

sources.title: Speak & Spell (toy)
sources.quote: The first Speak & Spell was introduced at the summer Consumer Electronics Show in 1978

note: Replaces second pass 2011 (Siri). Speak & Spell and talking chess/bridge computers (Popular Electronics ads and reviews 1980) were bought by ordinary families years before Siri; the year is a judgment (introduction 1978, routine household use evident by 1980-81) because no sales figure could be fetched. Strict reading (open-ended text-to-speech, a computer reading out answers) would point to later dates (e.g. Macintosh MacInTalk 1984, Siri 2011); I rejected that because the definition only asks for a machine that generates spoken language.
searched: ia_search3 'Speak & Spell' synthesized voice 1978-81 (Popular Electronics, ERIC, On Computing); Wikipedia Speak & Spell. Popular Electronics items gave 401/403 on read.

concept_note: First demonstration kept (1791) but now with the contemporary Kempelen book; first practical use kept at 1976 (earlier Votrax sales 1972 noted, not documented as end use); mass adoption moved from Siri 2011 to Speak & Spell c.1980 (low confidence, judgment).

what: Tiger Electronics showed the working Furby, an electronic robotic pet toy that reacts to touch, light and sound and 'learns' to speak, to buyers and press at the American International Toy Fair in New York.
fit: A small motorised, sensor-equipped robot built to act as an affectionate pet-like companion that responds to its owner, which is a loose but real match to a robot built for companionship (no romance or sex function).

sources.publisher: Mary Beth's Beanie World: Furby Edition
sources.title: Mary Beth's Beanie World: Furby Edition
sources.quote: completed the sam- ple Furby just in time for the annual eight day Toy Fair festival held in New York

sources.title: Furby
sources.quote: Furby's first public appearance was at the 1998 American International Toy Fair held in New York City.

note: Replaces second pass 1999-05 (AIBO). Furby (Feb 1998 Toy Fair) is earlier and is a robotic pet toy; I accept it as a companion robot but the fit is loose (a talking, moving toy rather than a sophisticated robot), so low confidence. If Furby is judged only a toy, the next fitting event is Sony's AIBO ERS-110, announced 1999-05-11. Paro was designed from 1993 but first exhibited only in late 2001; Elektro/Sparko 1939 were exhibits; Omnibot (1984) and Teddy Ruxpin (1985) were toy robots/animatronics sold for play, not marketed as companions. RealDoll (1996-97) is a doll, not a robot; no earlier romance or sex robot found.
searched: ia_search3 'robot pet / robotic pet', 'robot dog toy companion', 'companion robot / robot companion' 1980-98 (mostly fiction); Furby Tiger Electronics 1998-99; Wikipedia Furby and Paro (robot); AIBO 1999 news.

what: Furby went on general sale in the United States (launched 2 October 1998, with a press event at FAO Schwarz, New York), selling 1.8 million in 1998.
fit: The robotic pet toy was bought and kept by ordinary families as a companion that responds to touch and sound.

sources.publisher: Mary Beth's Beanie World: Furby Edition
sources.title: Mary Beth's Beanie World: Furby Edition
sources.quote: for his grand arrival at the flagship FAO Schwarz store in early October

sources.title: Furby
sources.quote: The product officially launched on October 2, 1998

note: Replaces second pass 1999-06-01 (AIBO sale; Sony's robot dog went on sale 1999-06-01, 3,000 units in Japan sold out in 20 minutes per a 1999-06-04 news item) because Furby was on sale eight months earlier. Same fit caveat as the demonstration. Paro handmade sales from 2004 are later.
searched: Same as demonstration; Atari Online News 1999-06-04 for AIBO sale date; Furby launch on Wikipedia and Beanie World.

what: Furby became a must-have toy: about 1.8 million sold in 1998 and 14 million in 1999, in homes across the US and other countries.
fit: Millions of ordinary households kept an interactive robotic pet toy as a companion.

sources.title: Furby
sources.quote: More than 40 million Furbies were sold during the three years of its original production, with 1.8 million sold in 1998 and 14 million in 1999.

note: No second-pass mass adoption existed. Date is 1999, when sales (14 million) made it common; 1998 was the holiday launch boom. Only a Wikipedia sales figure was fetched. A stricter 'robot' reading would put mass adoption at later robot pets (AIBO sold in thousands, 1999-2006) or none.
searched: Wikipedia Furby; ia_search3 Furby sales 1998-99 (no contemporary sales page readable; two Furby books gave 403).

concept_note: Second pass had AIBO 1999 for demonstration and use and no mass adoption; Furby (Feb 1998 Toy Fair, Oct 1998 sale, 14M sold in 1999) is earlier and counted as a robotic pet toy, low confidence because the fit is loose. No romance or sex robot found before these.

what: Edward L. Withey (Instrument Research Co., Brighton, Mass.) described an experimental cathode-ray tube, the Peritron, whose phosphor screen oscillates in depth inside a vacuum globe so that moving spots appear at true positions in three dimensions (proposed for air-traffic control).
fit: A volumetric display, not a hologram: a swept-screen CRT that draws changing points in a real 3-D volume seen in a viewing globe, so the picture is a true volumetric one rather than a stereo pair; the definition's 'holographic' wording is only its label.

sources.title: Cathode-Ray Tube Adds Third Dimension
sources.quote: Data can be pre.sented in true three dimen.nion.s with an ex¬ perimental cathode-ray tube called the I’eritron.

sources.title: Volumetric display
sources.quote: Although first postulated in 1912, and a staple of science fiction, volumetric displays are not widely used in everyday life.

note: Replaces second pass 1962 (static optical holograms), which the definition and test cases exclude (a static hologram is not a display of changing images). Candidates rejected: Parker/Wallis 'Three-dimensional cathode-ray tube displays' (IEE 1948) and MacKay's 'projective' displays (1949) only rotate a 3-D plot into a 2-D view, no volumetric picture; the 1962 optical holograms and Cross's 1972 multiplex hologram are static or fixed-sequence recordings; Traub's varifocal-mirror display (Applied Optics, 1967-06) and ITT's rotating-screen air-traffic display (Aviation Week 1960-10-31, 'gives 3-D effect from any viewing angle without need for stereoscopic illusion', working small-scale model) are later but clearly fit. Earlier volumetric proposals exist (1912 postulate) but no working device was found before Withey's.
searched: ia_search3 'three-dimensional display' rotating screen / varifocal mirror 1958-69 and 1945-59; Parker Wallis 1947-50; Withey 1957-59 (Electronics 1958 index); Crossref for Parker-Wallis 1948 and Traub 1967 (no abstracts); Wikipedia Volumetric display. Search hint on changing 3-D images viewable without glasses answered by the volumetric displays above.

what: The Actuality Systems Perspecta Spatial 3D volumetric display was integrated with a clinical radiation-therapy planning system (Pinnacle) so that planners could view patient anatomy and beams in 3D from any side.
fit: A swept-volume display showing changing patient-derived 3-D images in a 25 cm volume viewable from any side, used for its real purpose in treatment planning.

sources.publisher: Journal of Applied Clinical Medical Physics (PMC)
sources.title: Application of a 3D volumetric display for radiation therapy treatment planning I: quality assurance procedures
sources.quote: volume that is viewable from any side, floating within a translucent dome

sources.publisher: Journal of Applied Clinical Medical Physics (PMC)
sources.title: Application of a 3D volumetric display for radiation therapy treatment planning I: quality assurance procedures
sources.quote: has been integrated with the Pinnacle TPS (Philips Medical Systems, Madison WI), for treatment planning

note: Replaces second pass 1972 (Cross's moving multiplex hologram, an art/exhibit piece). The date is that of the clinical paper; a web search suggests the first Perspecta was delivered to the NIH Clinical Center in January 2004 (AuntMinnie, host blocked) and 2002 sales to universities for research, so real use probably began about 2002-2004, but I could not fetch a dated source. No earlier use outside the lab found for ITT's 1960 rotating-screen display (only a working model) or Withey's Peritron. Zebra Imaging's printed holographic maps for the US military are static, so excluded.
searched: WebSearch for Perspecta first customers; PMC article; AuntMinnie, Information Display (Actuality story) and OPN pages timed out or were refused by the egress proxy; ia_search3 for Perspecta 2001-04 (0 hits).

concept_note: Static holograms (1962) rejected as not a display of changing images; first demonstration moved to the 1958 Peritron volumetric CRT (low confidence, earliest working volumetric display found); first practical use moved from 1972 to the Perspecta medical-planning display (dated 2009 by the only fetchable source, real start c.2002-04). No mass adoption: neither holographic nor volumetric displays have become common.

what: Claude Shannon at Bell Labs built Theseus, a relay-driven magnetic 'mouse' that explored a rearrangeable maze by trial and error and then ran straight to the goal on the next trial (13 s against 2 min 10 s), re-learning when the maze was changed.
fit: A machine improved its performance from experience (its relay memory of the maze it had explored) instead of being programmed with the maze.

sources.title: Shannon and his maze-solving mechanical mouse
sources.quote: The mighty mouse had remembered the maze perfectly!

sources.title: Maze for Mechanical Mouse
sources.quote: After one exploratory trial, the mouse “remembers” exactly how to proceed directly to the goal.

sources.title: Claude Shannon
sources.quote: In 1950, Shannon designed and built, with the help of his wife, Betty, a learning machine named Theseus.

note: Moves the second pass's 1951 (SNARC) back to 1950 (Theseus, built 1950; shown at the 1951 Macy cybernetics conference and in Bell Labs press in 1952). SNARC (Minsky and Edmonds, summer 1951) is later and was reported only on Wikipedia. Other candidates: Ashby's Homeostat 1948 (adapts to disturbances by random search for stability, closer to self-regulation, rejected), Grey Walter's tortoises 1948 (no learning; his conditioned-reflex version is 1951), Samuel's checkers program (1952 running, 1959 paper), Rosenblatt's perceptron 1957-58, Thomas Ross's 1930s maze-solving machine discussed in Psychological Review 1935 (could not read a description in the available text, so not used). Exact month of first demonstration not established.
searched: ia_search3 Shannon maze mouse 1950-54 (Popular Science, Science News Letter, Mexican Life, Astounding); learning machine/Walter 1950-53; Ross 'Machines that think' 1935-40 (Psychological Review, unreadable); Ashby homeostat 1948-53 (0 hits); Wikipedia Claude Shannon.

concept_note: First demonstration moved earlier from SNARC 1951 to Shannon's Theseus 1950, now with two contemporary sources. No first_practical_use or mass_adoption: candidates (Widrow-Hoff adaptive filters and Lucky's adaptive equalizers of 1965-67, Bell Labs echo cancellers, spam filters c.2002) are adaptive signal processing or too diffuse, and I found no fetchable source dating a first use outside the lab or a year machine learning became routine.

what: Hideo Kodama (Nagoya Municipal Industrial Research Institute) built three machines that fabricated solid plastic models by exposing liquid photo-hardening polymer to UV light and stacking the solidified cross-sections; his papers appeared in 1981.
fit: An automatic machine built a solid object layer by layer by solidifying material cross-section by cross-section (mask or scanning-fibre exposure, an XYZ plotter), though whether the layers came from a digital design file is not stated.

sources.title: Automatic method for fabricating a three-dimensional plastic model with photo-hardening polymer
sources.quote: A solid model is fabricated by exposing liquid photo-hardening polymer to ultraviolet rays, and stacking the cross-sectional solidified layers.

sources.title: 3D printing
sources.quote: He filed a patent for this XYZ plotter, which was published on 10 November 1981.

note: Same event as the second pass, now with Kodama's own 1981 paper (abstract) as contemporary source; the date is 1981 only (Wikipedia gives April for the first paper and the apparatus work as April 1980; the Review of Scientific Instruments paper is November 1981). The paper itself says the operation 'can be easily automated', so full automation from a digital design is not certain; if that is judged essential, the next fit is Chuck Hull's first stereolithography part (1983, CAD-driven; patent 1984, granted 1986), which I did not source. Earlier candidates rejected: Willème's photosculpture (1860, not layered additive from a design), Swainson / Ciraud / Housholder patents of 1971-79 (patents, no demonstration), Raytheon 1982 powder patent (later).
searched: Crossref for Kodama (abstract), Wikipedia 3D printing and Stereolithography, ia_search3 stereolithography 1986-90; patents only seen via Wikipedia.

what: 3D Systems announced its stereolithography system (laser-cured acrylic resin, computer-controlled platform) as a product letting architects make detailed building models in minutes (Progressive Architecture, May 1987).
fit: A commercial machine built solid models automatically from computer sections of a design, layer by layer in photo-curing resin, for real design work.

sources.title: New Products: Model-building Electronically (3D Systems, Inc.)
sources.quote: A combination of computer graphics, lasers, and radiation chemistry now enables architects to create, in minutes, highly de- tailed, three-dimensional acrylic models of buildings.

sources.title: Stereolithography
sources.quote: After the patent was granted in 1986, Hull co-founded the world's first 3D printing company, 3D Systems, to commercialize it.

note: Second pass had 1987 from memory (SLA-1) with a Wikipedia source that only supports commercialisation after 1986; now confirmed by a 1987 trade-press product notice. Earlier internal use at Hull's firm (1983-86) and any earlier lab use of Kodama's machine were not documented as outside-the-lab service.
searched: ia_search3 'stereolithography 3D Systems Hull' 1987-90 and 'stereolithography laser resin' 1986-88; Progressive Architecture May 1987 read.

concept_note: First demonstration kept at 1981 (Kodama) with a contemporary source; first practical use confirmed as 1987 by a contemporary product notice. No mass_adoption: consumer desktop printers (2009 on) and dental/hearing-aid manufacture are real but I found no fetchable source dating a year when ordinary people used 3D printing routinely.
